title: Elodie and the Tide
premise: Jude Thackeray, a wedding planner whose own engagement ended in a courthouse and a lie, has spent ten years answering anonymous letters left in the tide-worn mailbox of a shuttered bakery on the Cornish coast. When Elodie Marsh—the woman who wrote those letters from a juvenile detention center, seeking the truth about her father's wrongful conviction—moves into the cottage next door, Jude's carefully invisible life begins to unravel. As Elodie reopens her father's case with evidence Jude unknowingly helped preserve, the two must decide whether loyalty to old promises matters more than the truth that could free a man or destroy them both. In the end, Elodie's father is exonerated, the bakery lease is signed under their joint names, and Jude, who never believed in second chances, stays past the last train.
about_author: W. M. Eriksen is the pen name of a former coastal archivist who spent years cataloguing letters found in abandoned buildings along the English shoreline. They write slow-burn romances about people who mistake silence for safety.

chapters.title: The Mailbox at Marrow Cove
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. A wedding collapses spectacularly when the groom confesses mid-vows, cementing Jude's cynicism. Driving home to Marrow Cove, they stop at the derelict bakery and find a new letter in the rusted mailbox—impossible, since the letters stopped ten years ago. The beat: unease beneath routine, the past knocking again.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Sent
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie arrives in Marrow Cove with a box of unsent replies and her father's case files, renting the cottage beside the bakery. She watches Jude through rain-streaked glass and recognizes the handwriting she's memorized for a decade. The beat: hope sharpened into intent—she didn't come for romance; she came for answers.

chapters.title: Neighborly
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The new neighbor introduces herself with flour-dusted hands and too many questions about the bakery. Jude deflects with professional charm but notices Elodie flinch at the word 'father.' That night Jude rereads the newest letter and realizes it matches the old ones exactly. The beat: suspicion blooming alongside unwanted attraction.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Flashback chapter: teenage Elodie writing her first letter to the stranger who once testified, wrongly, against her father—a baker who took the blame for a fire he didn't set. She explains how the correspondence became her lifeline, and why she stopped when the replies turned evasive. The beat: grief reframed as devotion.

chapters.title: The Wedding Nobody Wants
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. A wealthy client hires Jude to plan an anniversary party at the cove, demanding the bakery be included as 'rustic charm.' Jude must negotiate access—and finds Elodie already inside, reading the ledgers Jude secretly kept. The beat: collision of secrets; Jude lies badly for the first time in years.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie confronts Jude with the ledgers: entries proving her father paid protection money to the real arsonist, a man now a town councilor. Jude admits only to keeping records, not to knowing why. The beat: betrayal and relief tangled—Jude was the letter-writer all along, and never said so.

chapters.title: Low Tide Confessions
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. On the exposed flats at midnight, truths surface: Jude wrote every reply out of guilt; Elodie came not for forgiveness but for testimony. They argue, then walk back together in silence closer than speech. The beat: the first honest thing between them is anger.

chapters.title: The Councilor's Garden Party
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude works the anniversary event where Councilor Harrow presides, watching him charm the town that convicted an innocent man. Elodie attends uninvited, and Harrow's smile falters at the sight of her—she has her mother's face. The beat: the antagonist knows she's here; the stakes turn personal and dangerous.

chapters.title: Bread and Ashes
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie bakes in the dead bakery's restored oven, recreating her father's recipes from memory while Jude watches, undone by the ordinary intimacy of it. Someone breaks in overnight and ransacks the office—but takes nothing except one ledger page. The beat: warmth interrupted by threat; someone else wants the truth buried.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude finally tells the whole story: at nineteen, coerced by police and Harrow's family, Jude gave false testimony identifying Elodie's father. Every letter since was penance. Elodie walks out without a word. The beat: the confession Jude owed and dreaded; love and justice become irreconcilable—for now.

chapters.title: Last Train Out
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie packs to leave, ticket bought, dignity intact. At the station she reads the final letter Jude slipped into her bag—not an apology but the missing ledger page plus a sworn statement naming Harrow. The train arrives; she doesn't board. The beat: choice over impulse; staying becomes an act of will, not weakness.

chapters.title: An Alliance of Liars
chapters.summary: Both POVs. They form an uneasy pact: Elodie brings legal strategy, Jude brings the town's trust and twenty years of client confidences that map Harrow's crimes. First target: the retired police sergeant who coached Jude's testimony. The beat: partnership forged from damage; tenderness forbidden by the work.

chapters.title: The Sergeant's Silence
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The dying sergeant agrees to recant on tape but only if Jude publicly admits perjury first—ruining Jude's business and name. Jude signs the affidavit that night. Elodie finds out and is furious at the cost, not the act. The beat: sacrifice made alone; the gap between devotion and permission.

chapters.title: Rustic Charm
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The anniversary party becomes cover: while guests dance, Elodie photographs Harrow's private papers in the bakery office he rented for the weekend. Jude covers her absence flawlessly, then nearly kisses her in the dark and pulls away. The beat: adrenaline intimacy; desire acknowledged and deferred.

chapters.title: Harrow's Offer
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Harrow corners Jude with an offer: silence and a generous settlement, or exposure of Jude's perjury plus a fabricated scandal. Jude records the conversation on an old dictaphone meant for wedding toasts. The beat: the villain shows his fear; Jude chooses the fight over the exit.

chapters.title: What Loyalty Costs
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie's mother arrives, begging her to stop—revealing she always knew Jude's testimony was coerced and stayed silent to protect Elodie from hope. Elodie must forgive the mother who chose despair and the planner who chose guilt. The beat: loyalty examined; truth as the only honest inheritance.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Both POVs. The Criminal Cases Review Commission hearing: the sergeant's tape, Jude's affidavit, the ledgers, and Harrow's recorded threats converge. Harrow's lawyer dissects Jude's credibility, and Jude answers with plain, ruinous honesty. The beat: climax of the justice plot; truth spoken without armor.

chapters.title: Verdict Weather
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Waiting days stretch while a storm floods the cove; Jude and Elodie shelter in the bakery, baking bread by generator light, saying everything the investigation forbade. News comes by phone: conviction quashed, Harrow arrested. The beat: joy arriving quietly, in flour and lamplight rather than fanfare.

chapters.title: Homecoming
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Elodie's father returns to Marrow Cove and stands in his ruined bakery. He thanks Jude without absolution—'You were a child they used'—and asks Elodie what she wants now, free of the case that defined her. The beat: release; identity rebuilt beyond grievance.

chapters.title: The Lease
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The bakery lease expires Friday. Elodie's father offers it to both women—together—as a working bakery and event space. Jude hesitates, certain they'll repeat the past; Elodie refuses to plan a future around Jude's fear. The beat: the romance's true proposal isn't marriage but shared ground.

chapters.title: A Wedding, After All
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude plans one last event: not a wedding but the bakery's reopening, where the town that condemned Elodie's father fills the room to apologize in person. Midway through, Jude abandons the schedule and says the truest toast of their career. The beat: cynicism surrendered publicly; love declared without ceremony.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Both POVs closing. Months later: bread sold out by noon, letters still arriving in the mailbox—now answered openly. Elodie asks Jude, half-teasing, whether they believe in second chances yet. The last train passes the window; neither moves toward it. The beat: resolution—timing was never the problem; staying was the choice.
